extracted.intended_audience: school and university administrators, Title IX coordinators, legal counsel, and other recipients of federal education funding responsible for Title IX compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and interpretive guidance to final Title IX regulations describing definitions, reporting requirements, standards for actionable harassment, recipient obligations (including supportive measures and grievance processes), and how constitutional (First Amendment) concerns interact with enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any person may report sexual harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.8(a) (expressly stating that any person may report sexual harassment by using any of the listed contact information for the Title IX Coordinator or by any other means that results in the Title IX Coordinator receiving the person's verbal or written report, and such a report may be made 'at any time (including during non-business hours) by using the telephone number or electronic mail address, or by mail to the office address, listed for the Title IX Coordinator.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must notify all students, employees, parents and guardians of elementary and secondary school students, and others of the Title IX Coordinator's contact information, including prominently displaying that contact information on the recipient's website. This ensures that all persons (not only complainants themselves) have a clear, accessible method of reporting sexual harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual knowledge includes notice to Title IX Coordinator
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.30 (defining 'actual knowledge') revised to state that 'notice' constituting actual knowledge includes, but is not limited to, a report to the Title IX Coordinator as described in §106.8(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recipient's actual knowledge triggering response obligations can arise from reports made to the Title IX Coordinator; other forms of notice may also constitute actual knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may initiate the grievance process
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may report sexual harassment, although only a complainant (or Title IX Coordinator) may initiate a grievance process by filing or signing a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between reporting (anyone) and initiating the formal grievance process (must be complainant or Title IX Coordinator). Recipients must offer supportive measures upon notice even if no formal complaint is filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures – definition and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.30 (defining 'supportive measures' as non-punitive, non-disciplinary, not unreasonably burdensome to the other party).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures must be implemented promptly and equitably; recipients should refrain from punishing or disciplining a respondent without following a grievance process that complies with §106.45. Supportive measures are distinct from disciplinary actions and should not be unreasonably burdensome to either party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sexual harassment includes Clery Act/VAWA offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: These final regulations expressly include four Clery Act/VAWA offenses as sexual harassment as defined in §106.30: Sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated offenses are treated as sexual harassment under Title IX and, in the regulatory approach, are not subject to First Amendment protection in the same way as other expressive activity; recipients must respond to such incidents accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quid pro quo harassment treated as sexual harassment regardless of severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quid pro quo harassment by a recipient's employee involves speech designed to compel conduct; the Department believes that a broad prohibition against an employee conditioning an educational benefit on participation in unwelcome sexual conduct does not present constitutional concerns and that quid pro quo harassment constitutes sexual harassment under §106.30, without being evaluated for severity, pervasiveness, and objective offensiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quid pro quo may occur explicitly or implicitly and does not require the employee to expressly state a bargain. The age and position of the complainant are relevant. Speech incidental to quid pro quo conduct is not protected where the conduct facilitates discriminatory abuse of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: No alteration-of-environment requirement for quid pro quo and listed offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Under these final regulations, quid pro quo harassment, sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking do not require a showing of alteration of the educational environment (unlike some Title VII formulations requiring alteration of the workplace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should assume that victims of quid pro quo or the enumerated Clery/VAWA offenses have been effectively denied equal access to education and must respond even absent proof of altered educational environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single instance of sexual assault triggers response obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: A single instance of sexual assault (which includes fondling) requires a recipient's prompt response, including offering the complainant supportive measures and informing the complainant of the option of filing a formal complaint. §106.30 (defining 'sexual harassment' to include 'sexual assault'); §106.44(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even isolated incidents that meet the statutory definition of sexual assault impose immediate obligations on recipients to offer supports and information about grievance options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual harassment includes sex-based nonsexual conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: As noted by some commenters, sex-based harassment includes unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature but also includes unwelcome conduct devoid of sexual content that targets a particular sex. The final regulations use the phrase 'sexual harassment' to encompass both unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature, and other forms of unwelcome conduct 'on the basis of sex.' §106.30 (defining 'sexual harassment').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating incidents, recipients must consider both conduct that is sexual in nature and conduct that, while not sexual, is motivated by or targets a person's sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Davis severe/pervasive/objectively offensive standard for peer harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Davis standard evaluates whether student-on-student sexual harassment is sufficiently severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive so as to deny a person equal access to education (i.e., rises to the level of actionable discrimination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department returns to the Davis definition verbatim for evaluating peer harassment: for peer-to-peer claims, severity, pervasiveness, and objective offensiveness remain the threshold for Title IX liability in that context, although the final regulations separately address categories (quid pro quo and enumerated criminal offenses) that do not require those elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient liability requires deliberate indifference with actual knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Davis, recipients are properly held liable in damages only where they are deliberately indifferent to sexual harassment, of which they have actual knowledge, that is so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it can be said to deprive the victims of access to the educational opportunities or benefits provided by the school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must avoid deliberate indifference once they have actual knowledge (including notice to the Title IX Coordinator). The interplay of actual knowledge, deliberate indifference, and the Davis threshold determines institutional liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect free speech and academic freedom; avoid overbroad rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters and case law emphasize that First Amendment interests are implicated when expression on public college campuses is regulated; broad prophylactic rules are forbidden because the First Amendment demands precision of regulation. The Department notes the need to protect free speech and academic freedom while responding to sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting and enforcing policies, recipients should take care not to adopt overly broad or vague harassment codes that could restrict protected speech; apply the Davis framework and case-law constraints to avoid unconstitutional overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and position of complainant relevant in quid pro quo determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining whether unwelcome sexual conduct is proposed, suggested, or directed at a complainant, by a recipient's employee, as part of the employee 'conditioning' an educational benefit on participation in the unwelcome conduct, does not require the employee to expressly tell the complainant that such a bargain is being proposed, and the age and position of the complainant is relevant to this determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elementary and secondary students are generally expected to submit to teachers' instructions, making it more likely they will interpret certain conduct as a conditioned bargain; recipients should consider contextual factors (age, authority relationship) in quid pro quo assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fondling defined as Clery Act sexual assault
rubrics_metrics.description: The one exception is the offense of 'fondling,' included in the Clery Act under the term 'sexual assault.' Under the Clery Act (referring to the FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting system), fondling is a sex offense that means the 'touching of the private body parts of another person for the purpose of sexual gratification, without the consent of the victim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fondling, as defined, is treated as sexual assault under the regulations; even conduct that some may view as 'less severe' can meet the statutory definition and thereby trigger recipient obligations.
